title: He Was Hit on the Helmet. He Vomited on the Pitch. He Hit the Winning Six Anyway.
excerpt: Bangladesh captain Mehidy Hasan Miraz batted through a concussion to seal his country's first-ever ODI series victory over Australia — a result 21 years in the making.
body:
He was struck on the side of his helmet by a Riley Meredith bouncer in the 34th over. He grabbed his head, dropped to his knees, and then vomited on the ground as the Bangladesh team physio and the Australian team doctor rushed out together. A stretcher was brought on. The crowd in Mirpur held its breath.

Mehidy Hasan Miraz did not leave.

Bangladesh's captain got back up, took guard, and batted on — through a diagnosed concussion, through the nausea, through the most pressurized chase of his career. He finished unbeaten on 22 off 22 balls, and he ended it the way he wanted to: by smashing a six off Meredith, the same bowler whose bouncer had nearly put him in an ambulance.

Bangladesh had beaten Australia in an ODI series for the first time in history.

Two Decades of Waiting

The scale of this achievement cannot be overstated. Bangladesh had not beaten Australia in any ODI format for 21 years before this series. The Australians, six-time ODI World Champions, had treated Bangladesh as a scheduling formality for two decades. That ended emphatically in Dhaka this week.

Bangladesh won the first ODI by 86 runs — their first victory over Australia since 2005. The second ODI, played on Thursday, confirmed the series with an unassailable 2-0 lead. This was not a narrow escape. This was a statement.

How Bangladesh Dismantled the Australians

In the second ODI, Bangladesh's pace attack set the tone immediately. Taskin Ahmed and Mustafizur Rahman reduced Australia to 0 for 3 in the second over — only the fourth instance in ODI history of a team losing three wickets without scoring. Matthew Short shouldered arms to a Taskin in-swinger that uprooted his stumps. Mustafizur then extracted edges from Cooper Connolly and Matt Renshaw in the same over.

Australia never recovered. They limped to 81 for 6 before Marnus Labuschagne (55 off 85) and Xavier Bartlett (52 off 48) mounted a seventh-wicket rescue, adding 103 runs. But Taskin came back for a devastating third spell, dismissing Bartlett and then bowling Adam Zampa on the very next ball, just missing a hat-trick. Australia were bowled out for 187 in 42 overs.

Rain delayed the chase by three hours, revising Bangladesh's target to 188 in 35 overs under DLS. The hosts lost opener Tanzid Hasan for a duck, but Soumya Sarkar and Najmul Hossain Shanto both scored 42 to steady the ship. When both fell, Towhid Hridoy (40 not out) joined his captain Mehidy, and together they shared an unbeaten 51-run stand that sealed it.

A Captain's Courage

After the match, Mehidy was sent to hospital for 24-hour observation. Bangladesh physio Bayjedul Islam Khan confirmed the concussion diagnosis. "He continued to play after being assessed in the middle," Khan said. "We have sent him to the hospital to assess the rest of his signs."

Taskin Ahmed, who took 3 for 33 from eight overs, praised his captain's decision to stay. "It was incredible of Miraz to bat in that condition. I think he took a quick decision that if he walks off, the new batter could be prone to making a mistake in that pressure situation."

Mehidy is expected to miss the third and final ODI on Sunday but should be available for the T20I series starting June 17.

What It Means Beyond Mirpur

For the South Asian cricket community in the US, UK, and Canada, this series win resonates beyond the scoreboard. Bangladesh cricket has long lived in the shadow of India, Pakistan, and Australia. This series — played with aggression, tactical clarity, and extraordinary courage — is the clearest signal yet that the Tigers are no longer content with plucky underdog status.

With the 2027 ODI World Cup approaching and Bangladesh building genuine pace depth around Taskin, Mustafizur, and the emerging Nahid Rana, this Dhaka series could mark the beginning of something larger. For the Bangladeshi diaspora watching from London, New York, and Toronto, the captain who refused to leave the crease has given them a moment they will not soon forget.
